In the [[statistical physics]] of [[Order and disorder#Quenched disorder|disordered system]]s, the '''random energy model''' is a [[toy model]] of a system with [[quenched disorder]], such as a [[spin glass]], having a first-order [[phase transition]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Mézard |first=Marc |url=https://web.stanford.edu/~montanar/RESEARCH/BOOK/partB.pdf |title=Information, physics, and computation |last2=Montanari |first2=Andrea |date=2009 |publisher=Oxford university press |isbn=978-0-19-857083-7 |series=Oxford graduate texts |location=Oxford |chapter=Chapter 5. The Random Energy Model}}</ref><ref>Michel Talagrand, ''Spin Glasses: A Challenge for Mathematicians'' (2003) Springer {{ISBN|978-3-540-00356-4}}</ref> It concerns the statistics of a collection of <math>N</math> spins (''i.e.'' degrees of freedom <math>\boldsymbol\sigma\equiv \{\sigma_i\}_{i=1}^N</math> that can take one of two possible values <math>\sigma_i=\pm 1</math>) so that the number of possible states for the system is <math>2^N</math>. The energies of such states are [[Independent and identically distributed random variables|independent and identically distributed]] Gaussian [[random variable]]s <math>E_x \sim \mathcal{N}(0,N/2)</math> with zero mean and a variance of <math>N/2</math>. Many properties of this model can be computed exactly. Its simplicity makes this model suitable for pedagogical introduction of concepts like [[quenched disorder]] and [[replica trick|replica symmetry]].

== Thermodynamic quantities ==
Critical energy per particle: <math>h_c = \sqrt{\ln 2}</math>.

Critical inverse temperature <math>\beta_c = 2\sqrt{\ln 2}</math>.

Partition function <math>Z(\beta) = \sum_s e^{-\beta H(s)}</math>, which at large <math>N</math> becomes <math>2^N \mathbb E_E[e^{-\beta E}]</math> when <math>\beta < \beta_c</math>, that is, condensation does not occur. When this is true, we say that it has the '''self-averaging property'''.



[[Free entropy]] per particle<math display="block">f(\beta) =  \lim_{N \to \infty} \frac 1N \ln Z = \begin{cases} \ln 2 + \frac 14 \beta^2 \quad & \beta < \beta_c, \\
\beta \sqrt{\ln 2} \quad & \beta > \beta_c \end{cases}</math>

Entropy per particle<math display="block">s(h) = \max_\beta(f(\beta) - \beta h) = \begin{cases} \ln 2 - h^2 \quad & h \in [-h_c, +h_c ], \\ 0 \quad & \text{else }\end{cases}</math>
== Condensation ==
When <math>\beta < \beta_c</math>, the [[Boltzmann distribution]] of the system is concentrated at energy-per-particle <math>h = -\beta/2</math>, of which there are <math>\sim e^{N(\ln 2 - \beta^2/4)}</math> states.

When <math>\beta > \beta_c</math>, the Boltzmann distribution of the system is concentrated at <math>h = -h_c </math>, and since the entropy per particle at that point is zero, the Boltzmann distribution is concentrated on a sub-exponential number of states. This is a phase transition called '''condensation'''.

=== Participation ===
Define the '''participation ratio''' as<math display="block">Y = \sum_E p_E^2 = \frac{\sum_E e^{-2\beta E}}{(\sum_E e^{-\beta E})^2}</math>The participation ratio measures the amount of condensation in the Boltzmann distribution. It can be interpreted as the probability that two randomly sampled states are exactly the same state. Indeed, it is precisely the [[Simpson index]], a commonly used [[diversity index]].

For each <math>N, \beta</math>, the participation ratio is a random variable determined by the energy levels.

When <math>\beta < \beta_c</math>, the system is not in the condensed phase, and so by [[Asymptotic equipartition property|asymptotic equipartition]], the Boltzmann distribution is asymptotically uniformly distributed over <math>\sim e^{N(\ln 2 - \beta^2/4)}</math> states. The participation ratio is then <math display="block">\sim e^{N(\ln 2 - \beta^2/4)} \times (e^{-N(\ln 2 - \beta^2/4)})^2 = e^{-N(\ln 2 - \beta^2/4)}</math>which decays exponentially to zero.

When <math>\beta > \beta_c</math>, the participation ratio satisfies<math display="block">\lim_{N\to\infty} \mathbb E [Y] = 1 - \frac{\beta_c}{\beta}</math>where the expectation is taken over all random energy levels.

==Comparison with other disordered systems==
The <math>r</math>-spin [[Spin glass#Infinite-range model|infinite-range model]], in which all <math>r</math>-spin sets interact with a random, independent, identically distributed interaction constant, becomes the random energy model in a suitably defined <math>r\to\infty</math> limit.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Derrida|first=Bernard|title=Random Energy Model: Limit of a Family of Disordered Models|date=14 July 1980|volume=45|series=Physical Review Letters|issue=2|pages=79–82|doi = 10.1103/PhysRevLett.45.79|bibcode = 1980PhRvL..45...79D |url=https://hal.archives-ouvertes.fr/hal-03285940/file/Random-energy%20model%20%20limit%20of%20a%20family%20of%20disordered%20models.pdf}}</ref>

More precisely, if the Hamiltonian of the model is defined by

: <math>
H(\boldsymbol\sigma)=\sum_{\{i_1,\ldots,i_r\}}J_{i_1,\ldots i_r} \sigma_{i_1} \cdots \sigma_{i_r},
</math>

where the sum runs over all <math>{N\choose r}</math> distinct sets of <math>r</math> indices, and, for each such set, <math>\{i_1,\ldots,i_r\}</math>, <math>J_{i_1,\ldots,i_r}</math> is an independent Gaussian variable of mean 0 and variance <math>J^2r!/(2 N^{r-1})</math>, the Random-Energy model is recovered in the <math>r\to\infty</math> limit.

== Derivation of thermodynamical quantities ==
As its name suggests, in the REM each microscopic state has an independent distribution of energy. For a particular realization of the disorder, <math>P(E) = \delta(E - H(\sigma))</math> where <math>\sigma=(\sigma_i)</math> refers to the individual spin configurations described by the state and <math>H(\sigma)</math> is the energy associated with it. The final extensive variables like the free energy need to be averaged over all realizations of the disorder, just as in the case of the [[Spin glass#Edwards–Anderson model|Edwards–Anderson model]]. Averaging <math>P(E)</math> over all possible realizations, we find that the probability that a given configuration of the disordered system has an energy equal to <math>E</math> is given by

: <math>
[P(E)] = \sqrt{\frac{1}{N\pi J^2}}\exp\left(-\dfrac{E^2}{J^2 N}\right),
</math>

where <math>[\cdots]</math> denotes the average over all realizations of the disorder. Moreover, the [[joint probability distribution]] of the energy values of two different microscopic configurations of the spins, <math>\sigma</math> and <math>\sigma'</math> factorizes:

: <math>
[P(E,E')]=[P(E)]\,[P(E')].
</math>

It can be seen that the probability of a given spin configuration only depends on the energy of that state and not on the individual spin configuration.<ref name=nishimori>{{cite book|last=Nishimori|first=Hidetoshi|title=Statistical Physics of Spin Glasses and Information Processing: An Introduction|year=2001|publisher=Oxford University Press|location=Oxford|isbn=9780198509400|pages=243}}</ref>

The entropy of the REM is given by<ref name="RE Model: Exact Solution">{{cite journal|last=Derrida|first=Bernard|title=Random-energy model: An exactly solvable model of disordered systems|journal=Physical Review B|date=1 September 1981|volume=24|series=Phys. Rev. B|issue=5|pages=2613–2626|doi=10.1103/PhysRevB.24.2613|bibcode = 1981PhRvB..24.2613D |url=https://hal.archives-ouvertes.fr/hal-03285956/file/Random-energy%20model%20%20An%20exactly%20solvable%20model%20of%20disordered%20systems.pdf}}</ref>

: <math>
S(E) = N\left[\log 2 - \left(\frac E {NJ}\right)^2\right]
</math>

for <math>|E| < NJ\sqrt{\log 2}</math>. However this expression only holds if the entropy per spin, <math>\lim_{N\to\infty}S(E)/N</math> is finite, i.e., when <math> |E|< -N J \sqrt{\log 2}.</math> Since <math>(1/T)=\partial S/\partial E</math>, this corresponds to <math>T>T_c=1/(2\sqrt{\log 2})</math>. For <math>T<T_c</math>, the system remains "frozen" in a small number of configurations of energy <math>E\simeq -N J \sqrt{\log 2}</math> and the entropy per spin vanishes in the [[thermodynamic limit]].
